newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmiris wary over future of new government.
newsitem.headline: Kashmiris wary over future of new government.

text.p: Many Kashmiris expressed cynicism and mistrust on Thursday over the fate of the troubled Indian state's first elected government in nearly a decade.
The moderate National Conference party of charismatic Farooq Abdullah swept 54 seats in the 87-member state assembly in polls last month, results showed. Six races were yet to be decided.
Abdullah, who campaigned on a plank of more autonomy for the state, was likely to be sworn in as chief minister on October 8.
But many in Srinagar, the summer capital of the Himalayan state, said they did not believe Abdullah's government would be able to quell separatism and win autonomy from New Delhi.
"The militants who are left now are the dedicated ones who really believe in jihad (holy war)," said industrialist Mushtaq Shah. "Their activity against the government will increase."
Abdullah has promised to deal sternly with armed guerrillas, but hopes to begin talks with unarmed separatists.

Shah said a separatist revolt that began in 1990 crippled the economy of mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state. Since then, the workforce at his construction steel firm has dwindled from 22 to just a handful.
Police and hospitals say at least 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence.
"Elections in which people are coerced to vote are not the right solution for the Kashmir problem," said Manzoor Ahmed, 34, who runs a clothing store on Residency Road.

Many voters in last month's elections said security forces had forced them to vote, which Indian authorities denied. The separatist All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) conference urged voters to boycott the polls.
"Farooq will not win autonomy from New Delhi," Ahmed said. "In fact, it will take away even more of our autonomy."

Under the Indian constitution, Kashmiris hold nominal charge of their affairs except for foreign relations, defence and communications. But since 1952, many Kashmiris say, New Delhi has gradually infringed on these powers.
Many political analysts interpreted the election, which saw the National Conference build a base in both the Hindu-dominated Jammu and the Buddhist Ladakh regions, as a vote for autonomy.
Farooq's new government might take measures to pacify the region for five or six years, Ahmed said, but then the demand for self-determination would again intensify.
Abdullah was chief minister in 1990 when New Delhi dismissed the government after the rebellion flared.
"Corruption will increase now," said Shah. "There were no opportunities to earn money for anyone in the last seven years."
But some pinned their hopes on Abdullah.
"This man is the only bridge between Kashmir and India," said Azad Ahmed, an electrical contractor.
